title: Applying raw linseed oil to an old pine piece
subtitle: Clean, sand, and oil a bare pine furniture piece with two or three coats of raw linseed oil for a natural, low-build protective finish
excerpt: How to apply raw linseed oil to unfinished or previously oiled pine furniture. Covers cleaning and sanding, applying thinned first and second coats, the drying time between coats, and the final appearance.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics (referenced, not reproduced). Newey and Drage, Practical Carpentry and Joinery (referenced, not reproduced). UK natural finishes trade practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: An unprocessed drying oil pressed from flax seeds. Penetrates into bare timber and cures by oxidation to form a flexible, natural finish. Dries much more slowly than boiled linseed oil (days rather than hours); the slow cure prevents surface skinning. Traditional pine and softwood finish.

content.text: penetrates into pine and dries to a flat, slightly warm finish that shows the grain without a surface film. The job is clean, sand, oil, wait, repeat. Patience is the requirement: each coat takes several days to cure before the next can go on.

Used rags and cloths with linseed oil can combust spontaneously. After use, spread rags flat outside to dry, or submerge in water in a sealed metal tin. Never bundle oil-soaked rags and leave them in a pile or a bin.

Remove any old wax with white spirit on a cloth. Sand the piece with 120-grit along the grain to remove any surface roughness, staining, or old finish. Finish with 180-grit to leave the surface smooth but not polished. Wipe off all sanding dust with a tack cloth or a damp cloth; linseed oil applied over dust will leave a gritty finish.

Thin the raw linseed oil for the first coat with about 10% white spirit or turpentine; this helps the oil penetrate into the pine rather than sitting on the surface. Apply with a brush or a clean cloth, working along the grain. Apply generously; the wood will absorb the oil quickly on the first coat. Wipe off any excess that has not been absorbed after 20 minutes. Leave to cure.

Allow the first coat to cure until the surface feels dry and non-tacky: with raw linseed oil in a warm room, this typically takes 3 to 5 days. If the surface still feels tacky after a week, wipe lightly with a cloth dampened in white spirit to remove excess surface oil that has not cured. Apply the second coat of undiluted oil in the same way, wiping off the excess. Allow to cure again before the third coat.

After two or three coats, the pine will have a soft, even sheen that shows the grain. The surface darkens slightly compared to bare pine and develops a patina with use. Re-oil every 12 to 18 months: clean with a lightly dampened cloth, sand lightly with 220-grit if the surface has roughened, and apply one coat of oil.

attrs.symptom: The surface is sticky weeks after applying the oil
attrs.cause: Too much oil applied at once, or the room was too cold or damp to allow the oil to cure.
attrs.fix: Wipe the surface with white spirit to remove the uncured oil. Work in a warmer, ventilated room. Apply future coats in thinner amounts, wiping off all excess within 20 minutes.

attrs.symptom: Oiled surface shows dark patches where the grain absorbed oil unevenly
attrs.cause: End grain or soft early-wood sections absorbed more oil than the face grain.
attrs.fix: This is normal and will even out over two or three coats. Apply extra oil to the lighter areas; let it absorb, then wipe off the excess.
